stances.claim: BBM's Cabinet nominations 'have been widely accepted even by the opposition (or what is left of it, after the massive mandate of the victors),' but the heads of executive departments must still be confirmed by a 'majority of all the members' of the Commission on Appointments -- composed of 12 senators and 12 congressmen with the Senate president as ex-officio chairman (voting only to break ties), elected by each House on proportional-representation basis from party-list-registered parties.

The constitutional list of officials subject to confirmation is exclusive: 'heads of the executive departments, ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, or officers of the armed forces from the rank of colonel or naval captain, and other officers whose appointments are vested in [the President] by the Constitution.' Officials with Cabinet rank but not heading portfolios (Lagdameo as special assistant; Angping as PMS head) are excluded -- as are higher-ranked officials like the Bangko Sentral governor.
VP Sara Duterte's confirmation is automatic as a 'matter of courtesy' due to her high elective standing; the President's assumption of the agriculture portfolio is not subject to confirmation at all.

Public scrutiny is the inescapable price of Cabinet service: long-forgotten enemies will surface old indiscretions; income tax payments, past activities, and private ventures will be dug into; questioning is 'not necessarily to probe the nominees' suitability for their jobs, but to be able to horse trade political and personal favors.'

Department heads must leave their professions, divest from businesses, disclose assets-liabilities-relatives (by blood and affinity) annually, live simply per constitutional requirement, and 'be ready to explain how they acquired their mansions and how they can afford to send their children abroad' -- observing transparency and accountability not as bureaucratic exercise but as the 'price of public service.'

Cabinet members can take ethical lessons from concrete models: the late Dr. Jovito R. Salonga, who dissolved his famous law office upon Cabinet swearing-in despite not being legally required to do so; Carlos Dominguez III on conflict-of-interest avoidance; Menardo Guevarra on business divestment -- 'It is not enough to serve well, it is equally important to communicate well.'

Cabinet members are 'alter egos' of the President: they 'speak for him and act on his behalf,' must 'instinctively know his mind, his driving force, and his inner self,' must 'share the same mindset, the same vision as he,' subordinate their personal ambitions, and 'march to the beat of a single drummer.' 'Teamwork is as essential as brainwork and hard work.'

notable_anecdotes: The Salonga benchmark: 'Upon being sworn in as a Cabinet member, he dissolved his famous law office. Though not required by law, Salonga gave up his only source of income to set a high ethical standard.' -- preserved as the gold-standard ethical-divestment model.

CJ's signature image of practical preparedness: Cabinet members 'would be well advised to carry always an iPad or even an old-fashioned memo book where the Constitution, anti-graft law, ethical standards law, and relevant portions of the Administrative Code would be readily available.' -- modeling the embodied-discipline ideal of public officials.

The media-scrutiny inventory: officials 'will be headlined, columned, broadcasted, texted, Twittered, YouTubed and Facebooked' -- a comprehensive list capturing the multimodal public-exposure reality and the description of Philippine media as 'the freest in the world.'

The alter-ego-and-single-drummer doctrine closing: Cabinet members must 'subordinate their personal ambitions and march to the beat of a single drummer. Teamwork is as essential as brainwork and hard work.' -- a CJ-signature triad combining teamwork, brainwork, and hard work.

one_paragraph_summary: After President Ferdinand 'Bongbong' Marcos Jr. swore in his Cabinet on June 30 -- aligned with his inaugural message of 'unity, hope, and no excuses' -- Panganiban explains the confirmation process. The Commission on Appointments (Article VI Section 18) is a political (not judicial) body of 12 senators and 12 congressmen with the Senate president as ex-officio chairman voting only to break ties, with members elected by each House 'on the basis of proportional representation from the political parties or organizations registered under the party-list system represented therein.' Only heads of executive departments, ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, and AFP officers from colonel/naval captain upward (plus other officers whose appointments are vested by the Constitution) need confirmation; the list is exclusive. Officials with Cabinet rank but not heading portfolios -- like special assistant Anton Lagdameo and Presidential Management Staff head Naida Angping -- are not subject to confirmation, and even higher-ranked officials like the Bangko Sentral governor are excluded. VP Sara Duterte is confirmed automatically as a matter of courtesy; BBM's assumption of the agriculture portfolio requires no confirmation. CJ then turns to the substantive demands of Cabinet service: public scrutiny will surface old indiscretions, dig into income tax payments and private ventures, and pursue horse-trading. Department heads must leave their professions, divest from businesses, disclose assets-liabilities-relatives (by blood and affinity) annually, live simply, and 'be ready to explain how they acquired their mansions and how they can afford to send their children abroad.' They would be 'well advised to carry always an iPad or even an old-fashioned memo book' with the Constitution, anti-graft law, ethical standards law, and relevant Administrative Code portions ready at hand. He offers three named exemplars: the late Dr. Jovito R. Salonga, who dissolved his famous law office upon Cabinet swearing-in to set a high ethical standard though not legally required; former finance secretary Carlos Dominguez III on avoiding conflicts of interest; and former justice secretary (now SolGen) Menardo Guevarra on business divestment. Cabinet members 'will be headlined, columned, broadcasted, texted, Twittered, YouTubed and Facebooked' by what CJ calls 'the freest [media] in the world' on 24/7 call. As 'alter egos' of the President, they 'speak for him and act on his behalf,' must 'instinctively know his mind, his driving force, and his inner self,' must 'subordinate their personal ambitions and march to the beat of a single drummer.' Teamwork, he closes, 'is as essential as brainwork and hard work.'
